name: Telegraf
license: MIT (agent); Telegraf Enterprise and the paid tier of Telegraf Controller are commercial
summary: InfluxData’s plugin-driven Go agent that collects metrics from systems, services and devices and writes them to InfluxDB, Prometheus, Kafka and hundreds of other targets.
intro: Telegraf is a single Go binary that runs as an agent on a server, a container host or an industrial gateway. A TOML file lists plugins of four kinds. On every `interval`, for example every 10 seconds, the agent asks each input for data: CPU and disk counters, a Prometheus endpoint, SNMP, Modbus or OPC UA devices, or messages arriving from MQTT and Kafka. Processors rename and transform what comes back, aggregators compute new values such as means and maxima over a time window, and on every `flush_interval` the outputs write batches to their destinations. Inside, everything is a metric in InfluxDB’s model: a measurement name, string tags, typed fields and a timestamp. Each output keeps unsent metrics in memory, up to `metric_buffer_limit`; when that fills, the oldest are overwritten.

Telegraf is MIT-licensed and made by InfluxData, the company behind InfluxDB, but it does not need InfluxDB. More than 400 plugins are compiled into the official binary; a custom build can include only the ones you use, and plugins in other languages run as separate programs through `execd`. InfluxData sells Telegraf Enterprise: Telegraf Controller, a self-hosted UI and API that manages configurations and watches the health of agent fleets, plus support. Controller’s free version handles up to 20 configurations and 100 reporting agents; paid packages start at $18,000 a year and scale with the number of agents (list price, checked 2026-10-06).
strengths: One static binary with no external dependencies, easy to put on servers, containers and gateways
Inputs for network and industrial gear as well as hosts: SNMP, gNMI, Modbus, OPC UA, Windows performance counters, SMART and Nvidia GPUs
Not tied to InfluxDB: outputs include Prometheus, Kafka, PostgreSQL and TimescaleDB, OpenTelemetry and plain files
Aggregators and processors cut volume at the edge, for example sending a one-minute mean instead of every reading
Predictable releases: four minor versions a year, with bug-fix releases every three weeks in between
limits: Built around metrics: everything becomes a measurement with tags and fields, so logs and traces fit less naturally, and its OpenTelemetry output sends metrics only
The default buffer is in memory: a long outage that fills `metric_buffer_limit` overwrites the oldest metrics, and a restart loses what is queued. The disk buffer added in 1.32 is still experimental
Plugins are compiled in: the official binary carries all of them, and adding a Go plugin means building your own binary (or running it outside through `execd`)
Central configuration and fleet health beyond 20 configurations and 100 agents is a paid InfluxData product

sections.title: Telegraf, Controller and Enterprise
sections.intro: The agent is the same everywhere. What InfluxData sells is a management layer on top of it. Prices are list prices checked on 2026-10-06.

items.name: Telegraf
items.text: The agent itself, with all 400+ plugins. You write and distribute its TOML files yourself.

items.name: Telegraf Controller, free version
items.text: A self-hosted UI and API with a visual config builder, role-based access and fleet health monitoring. Up to 20 configurations and 100 reporting agents.

items.name: Telegraf Enterprise
items.text: Controller for larger fleets, with features such as high-availability clustering and audit logging, plus enterprise support. Licensed annually and priced by the number of agents under management. Generally available since June 2026.

story: In 2015 there was no shortage of agents that could feed InfluxDB: many users ran collectd or Diamond. But those tools were not designed around InfluxDB’s data model of measurements and tags, and InfluxData wanted a collector it could keep extending, perhaps with StatsD-style aggregation or alerting at the point of collection. Evan Phoenix and his company Vektra wrote the first version. Paul Dix made the repository’s initial commit in April 2015, and InfluxData announced Telegraf that June.

It was written in Go, with the code organised so that anyone could add a plugin for a new service or API. At launch it collected system metrics plus Docker, Redis, MySQL and PostgreSQL. Telegraf was the T of what InfluxData called the TICK stack, named after a tick, a single point in a financial time series.

Community plugins turned it into a general-purpose agent: more than 1,200 people have contributed, and its outputs reach far beyond InfluxDB. Version 1.0 was tagged in September 2016. In 2026 InfluxData added a paid fleet-management layer, Telegraf Enterprise, while the agent stays MIT.

choices.why: Measurements, tags, fields and a timestamp map one-to-one onto InfluxDB line protocol, so metrics arrive in InfluxDB without translation, while other outputs serialise them into their own formats.

choices.choice: Go, compiled into one static binary
choices.why: A binary with no external dependencies is easy to deploy anywhere, and Go code organised around plugins made it simple for outside contributors to add new inputs and outputs.

choices.choice: Plugins inside the binary, external ones through `execd`
choices.why: Built-in plugins must be Go. External programs can be written in any language and carry large or licensed dependencies that would otherwise bloat Telegraf for everyone.
